title: Delay is the cure
hookLine: the best cure for anger is delay (On Anger 2.29)

cards: The email arrives at 4:52 on a Friday. It's unfair, it's wrong, and it copies your boss. Your fingers are already typing.
The reply is excellent: sharp, true, and it would feel wonderful to send. Replies like that get written every day. Some get sent.
Deep in the second book of On Anger, Seneca gives what he calls the greatest remedy for it, and it's almost disappointingly simple. Not a technique. Not a philosophy.

teach.b: First, the line. The greatest remedy for anger is delay. Ask anger for time, Seneca says, not so that it will forgive, but so that it can judge.
Its first rush is heavy; if it waits, it eases. You don't have to win the argument with anger, only outlast its first wave.
Second, not all at once. Trying to rip anger out by force in the first moment rarely works. Picking it apart a little at a time does.
Third, while you wait, judge. Much of our anger, Seneca says, rests on things we believed too quickly: a rumor, a look, a tone of voice in a message.
Delay gives you time to ask the other side, check the facts, wonder whether there's a story you don't know. An angry reply can collapse under one question. Fourth, a teacher we've met.
Remember Athenodorus, who advised serving where you can? Possibly the same man; some readers think so.

The later writer Plutarch says that when Athenodorus left the court of the emperor Augustus, his parting advice was: when you're angry, don't say or do anything until you've recited the alphabet to yourself.

Twenty-four Greek letters, a delay you can carry anywhere. The week, looking back: calm is catching, mind your own business, read, don't display, put the seriousness down, finish the game, the body knows first.
Seneca's tools are rarely dramatic. A friend, a plain shelf, a game, a breath, and now, a pause.

how: Some readers of Seneca set a rule to wait before acting or replying in anger, sometimes an hour, sometimes a night, to let the first rush pass.

o: a burst of anger that clears the air
delay: giving anger time before you act
a fixed rule about when anger is allowed

games.q: delay is the cure — tap the pairs.

s: Seneca says ask anger for time so that it will forgive
so that it can judge; forgiveness may or may not follow.
Plutarch says Athenodorus advised Augustus to recite the alphabet when angry
Seneca says rip anger out all at once
he says pick it apart a little at a time; wait, and it loosens.

games.q: an unfair email arrives on Friday afternoon, copying your boss. your reply is ready. what does Seneca's remedy say?
o: wait; let the first rush pass, then judge.
games.why: delay, he says, is the greatest remedy: anger's first wave is heavy and passes if it waits.

practice: Think of a reply you're tempted to send while you're still hot, and picture putting it in a drawer, a version folder, an envelope. Breathe through whatever the waiting is like, itchy, unfinished, a little relieved.
While you breathe, ask the question you skipped: what might I not know about this?

wordCard.voice: Mora. Latin for delay: Seneca's greatest remedy for anger. Give it time, not to forgive, but to judge. Its first rush passes. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: delay. Twenty-four Greek letters are always there, within easy reach. That's a week, well spent.
